taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes N. louisianensis is treated as a distinct species by some authors and as a subspecies by others; a Hiwassee drainage population may be two species.
fieldMarks: Permanently aquatic salamander, 20-33 cm (MDC: usually 8-13 in, up to about 19 in) with large maroon external gills kept for life.
Grey, rusty brown to nearly black with black or blue-black spots or blotches; belly whitish to grey, sometimes spotted.
Hellbenders lose external gills by 4-5 inches; mudpuppies keep them.
behavior: Fully aquatic and usually nocturnal, though it may be active by day in murky or weedy water.
Solitary; active all year and does not hibernate; moves deeper in winter and summer, shallower in spring and fall; breeds in fall.
Eats crayfish, insect larvae, small fish, fish eggs, worms, snails and carrion, and is often caught on baited lines or traps.
habitat: Rivers, weedy ponds, large lakes and perennial streams with shelter; hides under logs, rocks or weeds by day; recorded to 30 m depth.
range: Southeastern Manitoba east to southern Quebec, south to Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, northern Kentucky, southern Illinois, central Missouri and south-central Kansas.

lookalikes.name: Red River mudpuppy
lookalikes.howToTell: Red River mudpuppy is smaller (max about 12 in) with more distinct spots and a pale unspotted central belly strip.
